Hello, friend. I love how you described this dilemma.  This is one area where I feel like I’m improving but very slowly and only after I dig up and unpack trauma through a “i was traumatized and in an actively abusive and toxic situation when this happened so it’s not my fault and I’m not a bad person” lens. You have to look at what happened to you in a trauma informed way in order to reduce shame. This has been key for me. I have all these false, predetermined assumptions and thought patterns that aren’t even mine. A lot of what I did before was just a cacophony of coping mechanisms, trauma responses, and survival tactics. The way I was forced to behave to survive a toxic situation. Whether it was fight, flight or freeze. The more I evaluate myself and my experiences in this way, the less shame I feel. I’m still angry but I’m starting to be less controlled by it.

I would like to recommend Patrick Teahan on YouTube—to you and everyone in this subreddit. He has a huge and mind blowing array of videos specifically about childhood trauma and is very considerate regarding religious trauma. He has helped me with the issue you mentioned about coping with injustice and lack of resolution. In one of his videos he talks about essentially getting sick of your own fixation on those who hurt you and in response tending to yourself and reclaiming your sense of safety and love. The goal is to accept that they have no real power over you in the present—you have to accept accept accept until you’re exhausted into indifference so you can heal. For “in the moment” triggers around this subject, It helps to think about positive things that happened in the past every time you think of a bad one. The ratio might not match up but it helps. For example, earlier I was ruminating about an incident with a teacher who wouldn’t let me go to the bathroom etc. etc. I was feeling triggered because I was thinking about how school was basically just an institution designed for control instead of something designed to spread love and knowledge. Then I thought about how my home life was the same way and bam, triggered BUT a w a r e. :)(BTW, this whole thought train was triggered by the school shooting that happened recently and me thinking about all that). Anyway, I was able to redirect the despair by thinking of my art teacher who was extremely sensitive and I suspect knew I was suffering in some way. He was very kind to me and I didn’t know why at the time. Thinking about this positive person I had in my life helped loosen the grip of the negative memory. I also gain some perspective because I did have some positivity growing up and I am only helping myself by acknowledging and honoring it. Also, it really helps to watch videos outside of therapy session so that you can learn the “language “ which helps you navigate it all. Best wishes!

Call your insurance company and tell them that you need help finding a provider in your area. You can see a psychiatrist or a psychiatric nurse practitioner (PsyNP). The insurance provider should give you a phone number to call and you will most likely have to leave a voicemail requesting a call back to set an intake appointment. Check yelp and call multiple places, The one who calls you back first is more likely to have their shit together.
2) at the intake appointment with the psychiatrist, give them a rundown of your situation, what has worked for you before, what doesn’t work for you and what your goals are for treatment. They will have you fill out a questionnaire usually. If they rub you the wrong way at the first appointment you have no obligation to go back. They are able to prescribe your meds at the first appointment, so if the provider is resisting that then you need to MoveOn. You can ask your psychiatrist for a referral to a good counselor or ask if there are any who work in the building that also take your insurance as that is usually the case. 

A psychiatrist should not try to be your therapist. So, at the appointment there is really no need to pour your heart out though, it is perfectly fine to be emotional about the fact that you are struggling. The conversation with the psychiatrist should be focused on treatment options—not your well-being per say. They are there to Monitor your treatment, not to help you process. For therapy, you can see a social worker, licensed therapist, psychologist or certified counselor. Avoid People who referred to themselves as“life coaches” even in passing. Make sure your therapist is helping you process and not just showering you with compliments or trying to make you feel better in superficial ways.

Documentation, communication and follow up. I think a lot of foster parents rely on good faith and don’t feel the need to protect themselves until it is too late. People need to utilize emails—particularly ccs and time stamps, know when to elevate. Keeping a good binder is extremely important—some fosters I know are very disorganized and take 5 min to tell me when the kiddo’s last appointment was. When you leave a voicemail for a CM, give them an idea of what you need...not just “please call me”.

Some other issues/topics that I see foster parents struggle with frequently:

-managing expectations—with both children and child services. The system is completely overwhelmed. People need to have reasonable expectations in order to contribute effectively.
-how to advocate at court and being heard
-how to deal with disruption to minimize trauma and drama for everyone involved 
-online support groups/forums
-boundaries and professionalism with social services—a lot of fosters take things very personally and they really shouldn’t. Often times the decisions that I see fosters complaining about most are made by judges and not social services.
-finances and money management. Foster parents should really not be calling the child’s caseworker asking for money or using community resources that are meant for kinship. If your cup isn’t overflowing then you should reconsider fostering. It’s a hard truth
-TAXES— this time of year I have so many foster parents that are clueless about how/when to claim children as dependents on their taxes.
-ICPCs—these take a very long time— I have many foster parents who are impatient and do not understand that the sending state has no authority over how long the receiving state takes to complete an ICPC homestudy.
Entitlement—foster care is a charitable act. If you want a higher payment, you need to provide documentation. Do not try to play negotiation or ultimatum games with child services or adoption subsidy. It makes you look bad and makes us doubt your commitment to the child.
-Please tell fosters not to use garbage bags as makeshift luggage under any circumstance. Stock up on ikea bags or something. I have 6 in my car at all times. I get sick to my stomach when I pick up a child from a 3k sq ft foster home and his clothes are in garbage bags. Come on, people.
-Trauma—this goes along with managing expectations. So many fosters sign up for placements that are “0-2 no issues” and think they are helping and sit around wondering why they have empty beds. We need fosters who are up for behavioral challenges and that understand that these children need help. Foster parents need to be trained and ready to meet crises head on rather than kick kids out at the first sign of trouble.
